description: Width tiers for History 7–10, Year 8. Covers all 24 descriptors: K01–K16 (Knowledge and Understanding) and S01–S08 (Inquiry Skills). Generated from ACARA v9 elaborations using width_generation_prompt.md v1.0.
subject: History

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest engagement that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. For K-strand: the smallest set of phenomena, contexts or examples that meets 'explain'. For S-strand: the narrowest task context in which the skill is applied. Minimum is not 'easy' — it is honest.
width_notes.typical_width: The full scope of the descriptor as ACARA intended it, grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Typical reflects a class that has engaged with the descriptor seriously — covering the elaboration range without necessarily exhausting it.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new phenomena, contexts or task types — not harder versions of the same thing. For K-strand: additional historical societies, periods, or cross-civilisational comparisons. For S-strand: additional task types, source types, or contexts in which the skill is applied. Two to four discrete directions per descriptor.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are used as source data, not a checklist. Typical_width is grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Wider may extend modestly beyond elaborations where the direction is clearly within the descriptor's territory. Elaborations are preserved verbatim in each width_entry as the source record.

AC9HH8K01.minimum_width: Identify two or more key events or developments that contributed to the transformation from the ancient to the early modern world (e.g. fall of Rome, spread of Christianity) and describe what changed as a result.
AC9HH8K01.typical_width: Explain the key transformations across the full elaboration range: decline of ancient empires and migration of peoples; the spread of Christianity and Islam; the development of the feudal system; the growth of towns and trade; the emergence of Renaissance ideas. Connect at least two of these developments to features of modern political, religious or cultural life (e.g. the Westminster system, the Magna Carta, religious holidays).
wider: Examine the historical significance of specific turning-point events — the conversion of Constantine (312 CE) and the invasion of England by William the Conqueror (1066) — as case studies in how individual events shaped the broader transformation

Investigate the role of Islamic scholarship in preserving classical texts and transmitting knowledge to Renaissance Europe, exploring how the spread of Islam and the European Renaissance were connected across civilisations
Trace the expansion of the Ottoman Empire as a case study in how Islamic political power intersected with trade and cultural exchange across the Mediterranean world

Explore the historical significance of Renaissance individuals who caused change — examining what conditions enabled their influence and what their achievements meant for the emergence of the modern world
elaborations: identifying the key events that have shaped the modern era, such as the decline of ancient empires and societies; the spread of Christianity in Europe; the spread of Islam through the Arab world, Mediterranean coast, Egypt, North Africa and Persia; the development of the feudal system; the growth of towns and cities; trade; the migration of peoples and the emergence of new ideas

describing the connection between key events or developments of this period to modern day life, such as religious holidays and political systems; for example, the expansion of the Ottoman Empire, the Magna Carta and the Westminster system
investigating the emergence of ideas about the world such as those formed during the Renaissance, and the place of significant individuals and people that caused change
explaining the historical significance of selected key events such as the conversion to Christianity of the Emperor Constantine in 312 CE and the invasion of England by William the Conqueror in 1066

AC9HH8K02.minimum_width: Describe the structure of feudal society — including the roles of at least three groups (e.g. king, Church, knights, peasants) and their responsibilities — and explain continuity or change in one area of medieval life.
AC9HH8K02.typical_width: Explain the structure and roles of feudal society across its main groups (king, nobles, Church, knights, peasants, men and women); describe continuity and change across at least two areas such as towns and commerce, farming and environment, or the spread of literacy; explain the contribution of key theories (Copernicus, Galileo, Newton) to the Scientific Revolution and how these changed medieval social and intellectual structures.
wider: Examine daily life in Renaissance Italy — the roles of men and women, the influence of city-state governance in Naples (monarchy) vs Florence (republic) — to show how urban contexts modified feudal social structures
Investigate the similarities and differences between the popolo minuto (common people) and popolo grasso (wealthy merchant class) in Renaissance Italy as a lens on emerging class differentiation
Explore the spread of Renaissance culture to England — including the rise of literature through Shakespeare — as evidence of how intellectual transformation moved across political borders

Examine the environmental impact of medieval society — harnessing water and wind power, urban settlements, management of royal forests — as an underexplored dimension of medieval social and political organisation
elaborations: describing the structure of feudal society, including the role and responsibilities of the king, nobles, church, knights, peasants, and women and men

explaining the continuities and changes in society in one of the following areas: crime and punishment; military and defence systems; towns, cities and commerce; farming and the impact on the environment such as tree clearance

explaining how medieval society changed and affected the environment; for example, harnessing water and wind power for milling, urban settlements and agriculture, management practices and legal structures of medieval forests such as the English royal forests

describing key changes of life in the late Medieval period such as the spread of literacy and the development of new ways to disseminate ideas through schools and universities, scientific academies, debating societies, literary salons, coffee houses, and the reach of printed books, journals and pamphlets
explaining reactions to the Black Death, such as the emergence of flagellants (those who would whip themselves to be free of sin) and the persecution of Jewish people
identifying the similarities and differences of daily life between the popolo minuto and popolo grasso

describing the way of life of people in Renaissance Italy; for example, the role of men in tending the fields or merchant shops, the role of women in the society and the influence of government in particular city-states such as Naples (a monarchy) and Florence (a republic)
identifying the spread of Renaissance culture to England; for example, the rise of literature through Shakespeare
The emergence of the modern world

describing the contribution of key theories such as Nicolaus Copernicus' De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, Galileo's Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems and Isaac Newton's Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica to the changes brought about by the Scientific Revolution

examining the changes in economic activity created by the discoveries of new commodities, making the costs of basic foodstuffs lower and the quality higher, and the advancements of technologies such as in tools, armaments and shipbuilding

AC9HH8K03.minimum_width: Explain a specific turning point (e.g. Black Death, Magna Carta, Crusades, printing press) — describing at least two causes and at least two effects — and explain how it contributed to continuity and change for at least one social group.
AC9HH8K03.typical_width: Explain the chosen turning point across its full causal and consequential range: immediate triggers and longer-term causes; effects across social, economic, religious and political domains; what changed and what continued for different groups. Use primary sources as evidence (e.g. artworks, manuscripts, church records, architectural evidence). Connect the turning point to at least one feature of the modern world.
wider: Investigate the effects of the Black Death in a specific city (e.g. Carthage, Damascus or Rome) using church records — examining labour shortages, peasant uprisings, weakening of feudal structures, and challenges to religious power as a multi-domain chain of consequence

Examine the significance of double-entry bookkeeping (Messari accounts of the Republic of Genoa, 1340) and the Catasto of 1427 in Florence as economic turning points within the period, exploring how financial innovation accelerated wealth production

Investigate the Enlightenment's ideas about human freedom and constitutional government as an ideological turning point — comparing how rulers in France, England, Spain and Russia responded differently to new and dissenting ideas
Examine the features of the French Ancien Régime — increasing centralisation of power in the monarchy — as a case study in how structural continuity can create the conditions for revolutionary change
elaborations: describing the features of castles and churches of the period, such as Warwick Castle in England and Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris, as examples of the Church's power in terms of its control of wealth, land and labour
examining the nature of illuminated manuscripts and recognising that the medieval manuscripts of monastic scribes contributed to the survival of many ancient Greek, Roman and Arab literary texts
explaining the changing relations between Islam and Europe, including the effects of the Crusades and trade
describing the impact of the Magna Carta on different social groups including the nobility, religious orders, merchants, workers/craftsmen, peasants and women

investigating the effects of the Black Death in a city such as Carthage, Damascus or Rome; for example, labour shortages, peasant uprisings, the weakening of feudal structures, increased social mobility, and challenges to religious ideas and power

identifying the effect of the Black Death on human populations using studies of church records from the period, considering the reliability of these statistics and explaining the impact of the population change in areas such as farming, commerce, culture and religion
describing the significance of double-entry bookkeeping, as seen in the Messari accounts of the Republic of Genoa in 1340 CE, in accelerating the production of wealth and patronage

investigating learning in the Renaissance period (for example, humanism and the influence of ancient Greece and Rome) and analysing the symbolic representation of this learning in architecture, artworks and inventions from individuals such as Brunelleschi, Copernicus, Donatello, da Vinci, Michelangelo and Titian
explaining why the Catasto of 1427 was introduced in Florence following the end of war with the Duchy of Milan
identifying a range of primary sources, such as artwork, music, literature, architecture, correspondence and diaries, that demonstrate the spread of the Renaissance across Europe
The emergence of the modern world
describing the impact of the printing press on the rise of literacy

investigating the Enlightenment ideas about human freedom and the exercise of authority, which promoted radical change to the political order; for example constitutional government and the separation of Church and state
examining how rulers in different European nations responded differently to new and dissenting ideas that were emerging by comparing the responses of France, England, Spain and Russia
investigating the way of life in key features of the French "Ancien Régime" and how it represented increasing centralisation of administrative power in the monarchy

AC9HH8K04.minimum_width: Explain how power was exercised by rulers in medieval Europe — using at least one primary source — and describe how at least two social groups experienced that power differently.
AC9HH8K04.typical_width: Explain the exercise and justification of power across medieval and early modern Europe: different punishments for different groups (e.g. trial by combat for nobility, ducking stools for women); the impact of the Black Death on daily life and rulers' responses; the differing political arrangements of Italian city-states (Florence, Venice, Naples, Papal States); how the bourgeoisie and peasant classes' power changed with urbanisation; the decline of absolutism and development of parliaments.
wider: Analyse primary sources (Matteo Villani's diary, Boccaccio's Decameron, Fordun's Chronicle, Ibn Khaldun's recollections) to understand how the Black Death disrupted the usual exercise of power and how different groups experienced that disruption
Examine the role of Oliver Cromwell and the execution of Charles I in the English Civil War as a case study in how the Westminster parliamentary system developed through conflict over royal authority

Investigate the Enlightenment's ideas about human freedom as an ideological challenge to medieval authority — comparing how France, England, Spain and Russia responded to produce different political trajectories

Examine the features of the French Ancien Régime as a case study in how the centralisation of monarchical power can simultaneously represent continuity and the conditions for revolutionary transformation
elaborations: explaining the reasons for different punishments for different groups of people, such as trial by combat as a privilege granted to the nobility and ducking stools as a punishment for women, and the use of punishment as a deterrent

describing the impact of the Black Death on daily life using primary sources such as Matteo Villani's diary, Boccaccio's Decameron, Fordun's Chronicle of the Scottish Nation and Ibn Khaldun's recollection of the impact of the plague
analysing how rulers responded to demands from the lower classes to improve their working conditions and lives following the plague, using sources such as King Edward III's law Statute of Labourers
analysing primary sources to understand the interactions between the rulers of Florence, Venice, Naples and/or the Papal States
explaining the differing levels of political involvement in city-states such as the guilds in Florence and Libro d'Oro in Venice
The emergence of the modern world

examining the change in the role and power of monarchies in the political systems of Western Europe, for example, decline of "absolutism", development of parliaments, and new ideas relating to nationalism
investigating the changes and continuities in the political power of the bourgeoise and peasant classes with the growth of cities and increased urbanisation, and the movement of peoples

AC9HH8K05.minimum_width: Explain the role and at least two achievements of one significant individual or group in Medieval, Renaissance or pre-modern Europe — using at least one source as evidence.
AC9HH8K05.typical_width: Explain the role, achievements and impact of the chosen individual or group across the elaboration range: the Catholic Church's influence and provision of social services; the Medici family as patrons and merchants; key Renaissance and Reformation individuals (Galileo, da Vinci, Machiavelli, Luther, Louis XIV, Lucrezia Borgia); the Scientific Revolution — Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler and Newton overturning traditional views; Oliver Cromwell and the development of the Westminster system.
wider: Examine the importance of the Scientific Revolution for overturning traditional views of planetary motion — and how this contributed to science being seen as an alternative to the Church as a source of fundamental truth about reality

Investigate the role and significance of Oliver Cromwell and the execution of Charles I in the development of the Westminster parliamentary system — tracing the achievement from the English Civil War to modern parliamentary democracy
Use visual sources such as the illustration of Hell in the Hortus Deliciarum (Herrad of Landsberg) to examine the Catholic Church's role in shaping beliefs and social control through imagery

Examine Lucrezia Borgia as a case study in how gender, political alliance and historiography intersect in assessing a significant individual's role — questioning whose achievements are remembered and whose are obscured
elaborations: explaining the influence and dominance of the Catholic Church on society using visual sources such as the illustration of Hell in the Hortus Deliciarum manuscript by Herrad of Landsberg
investigating the role of the Catholic Church in Medieval Europe in the provision of social services such as education, health care and social welfare, and in feudal village organisation
explaining the influence of the Medici family in Florence as bankers and merchants, and their patronage of the arts
explaining the influences and contributions of individuals such as Lucrezia Borgia, Galileo, Leonardo da Vinci, Niccolo Machiavelli, Martin Luther and Louis XIV
The emergence of the modern world
investigating the role and achievements of Henry VIII, Elizabeth I and Martin Luther

investigating the importance of the Scientific Revolution, in particular the scientific theories and discoveries of Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler and Newton, for overturning traditional views of the motion of the planets, and how these contributed to science being seen by many as an alternative to the Church as a source of fundamental truth about reality
investigating the role and significance of Oliver Cromwell and the execution of Charles I in the English Civil War in the development of the Westminster parliamentary system

AC9HH8K06.minimum_width: Describe two different historical interpretations of an event, individual, group, institution or movement in Medieval, Renaissance or pre-modern Europe — and explain at least one reason why they differ.
AC9HH8K06.typical_width: Explain how and why historians have developed different interpretations across the period: how medieval myths (King Arthur, Pope Joan) have been disproved; why the Black Death has been misconceived as primarily European; the importance of Renaissance women (Caterina Sforza, Isabella d'Este, Lucrezia Borgia, Catherine de Medici) as reassessed through artwork and historians' interpretations; how interpretations of the Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment highlight their importance to contemporary society.
wider: Analyse the importance of key Renaissance women using artwork, written sources and historians' interpretations — examining how gendered assumptions shaped earlier historical accounts and how revisionist interpretations have changed our understanding

Examine how the interpretations of the Enlightenment and Scientific Revolution have been linked to ideas about human reason and progress — and evaluate how much weight to give contemporary relevance as a criterion when assessing historical significance
Investigate how historians have disproved medieval myths (King Arthur, Pope Joan) as a case study in how the discipline of history uses evidence to correct popular misunderstanding
Explore how post-colonial perspectives have changed interpretations of the period — examining whose experiences were centred in earlier historiography and whose were marginalised
elaborations: explaining how historians have disproved medieval myths such as King Arthur or Pope Joan
analysing why the Black Death has been misconceived as impacting Europe predominantly, with reference to differing historians' interpretations

analysing the importance of key women in Renaissance society, such as Caterina Sforza (1463–1509), Isabella d'Este (1474–1539), Lucrezia Borgia (1480–1519) and Catherine de Medici (1519–1589), using a range of artwork, written sources and historians' interpretations to justify claims
The emergence of the modern world

explaining how the interpretations of the discoveries of science are linked to ideas about the free exercise of human reason and how that could lead to improvements and progress in human life and society generally

examining historical interpretations of key events, developments or achievements during this period, such as the Scientific Revolution or the beginnings of the Age of Reason/Enlightenment, and how these interpretations highlight their importance or significance to contemporary society

AC9HH8K07.minimum_width: Describe at least two significant social, cultural, economic or political features of one group connected to empire or expansion (Mongols, Ottomans, Vikings or Aztecs) — explaining how these features shaped their way of life.
AC9HH8K07.typical_width: Explain the significant features of the chosen group across social, religious, cultural, economic and environmental dimensions, grounded in primary source evidence where possible. Cover the elaboration range for the chosen context: for Mongols — nomadic life, animal domestication, Genghis Khan's rise; for Ottomans — coffee house, bazaar, Sultan's authority, primary source tracking across time; for Vikings — environment, farming, raiding, honour culture, gender; for Aztecs — social organisation (nobility, slaves), religious beliefs, Tenochtitlan.
wider: For the Mongols: examine how facets of Mongol life (horses, camels, yurts, dried meat, yoghurt) were incorporated into Chinese life after conquest — showing how expansion transformed both the conquerors and the conquered
For the Ottomans: use primary sources to track changes in way of life across different times or locations within the empire, examining how Ottoman society varied by place and period
For the Vikings: investigate how the environment of Scandinavian Viking lands directly influenced the activities — farming limitations, coastal access — that drove expansion beyond Scandinavia
For the Aztecs: examine the social and political functions of religious practices (e.g. human sacrifice as state ritual) to understand how religion underwrote political authority in Tenochtitlan
elaborations: describing the nomadic nature of Mongol life and how it enabled the rise of Temujin (Genghis Khan), who united all Mongol tribes in 1206 CE

describing facets of life in Mongolia and the incorporation of these facets into Chinese life; for example, agriculture – domestication of animals such as horses, camels and cattle; food – dried meat and yoghurt; housing – yurts

describing the way of life of people in the Ottoman Empire; for example, the role of women, the role of the coffee house and bazaar or marketplace, and the power and responsibility of the Sultan to ensure that justice was served within society
using a selection of primary sources to track changes in the way of life in the Ottoman Empire across time or locations

describing the way of life of the Vikings; for example, living in a cold and harsh environment, the importance of farming and raids, the significance of honour in Viking warrior society and the role of gender
explaining how the environment of Viking lands in Scandinavia influenced the activities of societies
The Spanish conquest of the Americas

describing pre-Columbian life in the Americas, including the social organisation of the Aztecs (for example, nobility and slaves), their beliefs (for example, worship of a number of gods and the need to make human sacrifices to appease these gods), and life in the capital city of Tenochtitlan

AC9HH8K08.minimum_width: Explain one significant turning point connected to empire or expansion — describing at least two causes and at least two effects for different groups — and explain how it contributed to continuity and change.
AC9HH8K08.typical_width: Explain the chosen turning point across its full causal and consequential range for the selected context: for Mongols — Genghis Khan's policies (decimal organisation, codified laws, religious freedom, trade expansion), Mongol connections between Europe and Asia; for Ottomans — role of warfare in territorial expansion, Islamic inventions and their adoption in the West, impact of the Crusades; for Vikings — longboat construction innovations, trade between Russia and the east, decline triggers (Stanford Bridge, climate change, Christianity); for Spanish conquest — arrival chronology (Balboa to Pizarro), papal decrees of 1493, effects on Indigenous populations.
wider: For the Spanish conquest: analyse the longer-term effects on Indigenous populations — unequal land distribution, slavery, political inequality, supremacy of Spanish culture and language — showing how a medieval turning point produced modern inequalities

For the Mongols: examine Genghis Khan's policies governing his empire (banning seasonal animal killing, supporting religious freedom, expanding trade) as evidence of a governing philosophy that made the empire administratively sustainable beyond conquest
For the Vikings: investigate evidence of Viking trade between Russia (Kiev) and the east through Constantinople as evidence of a turning point from raiding culture to trading civilisation

For the Ottomans: examine Islamic inventions and developments (astrolabe, public hospitals and libraries) and their adoption in the Western world — showing how the Ottoman Empire's turning points in knowledge and technology had cross-civilisational impact
elaborations: explaining the role of the Mongols in forging connections between Europe and Asia through conquest, settlement and trade; for example, the use of paper money and coinage; the growing number of European merchants travelling to China

explaining Genghis Khan's use of decimal organisation in his army and his policies for governing his empire, including codifying laws, banning the killing of animals in the breeding season, supporting religious freedom and expanding trade
analysing the effects of Mongol expansion including life in China before, during and after the Mongol conquest
explaining the role of warfare in expanding Ottoman territory, including the sieges of Bursa (1317–1326 CE) and Nicaea (1328–1331 CE)
describing Ottoman art and architecture, such as Selimiye Mosque in the city of Edirne in Turkey, and Islamic geometric design
outlining inventions and developments in the Islamic world, such as the astrolabe, public hospitals and libraries, and their subsequent adoption in the Western world
explaining the impact of the Crusades in challenging the Ottoman Empire and the responses of the Ottomans to the challenge
identifying the key role of gods such as Odin, Thor, Frey and Freyja in Viking religion and the impact of the adoption of Christianity during the Viking period
explaining the significance of the construction of longboats and their role in exploration, including innovations in keel and sail design
identifying and analysing evidence of Viking trade between Russia (Kiev) and the east (through Constantinople)
describing Viking craft with particular emphasis on the production of weapons and armour (for example, swords, battle axes and helmets) and the effectiveness of these in battle
explaining the triggers of declining Viking power such as the Battle of Standford Bridge, the treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, new colonies, changing climate and/or the spread of Christianity
The Spanish conquest of the Americas

explaining the arrival of Spanish conquistadores in Mexico and Peru from 1510 CE (Balboa) to 1531 (Pizarro), and their reasons; for example, seeking wealth, claiming land for their king, converting the local populations to Christianity, sense of adventure
analysing the significance of Alexander VI's papal decrees of 1493 in legalising Spanish territorial expansion and claims in the Americas

outlining the effects of Spanish conquest on the Americas, such as the spread of disease, introduction of crops such as maize, beans, tobacco, chocolate and potatoes to Europe, the Encomienda system, mining and deforestation, and the impact of the loss of natural resources

explaining the longer-term effects of conquest and colonisation on the Indigenous populations of the Americas, such as the unequal distribution of land and wealth, slavery, political inequality, and supremacy of Spanish culture and language over conquered territories

AC9HH8K09.minimum_width: Describe how rulers in one empire exercised power — using at least one source as evidence — and explain how at least one subject group experienced that power.
AC9HH8K09.typical_width: Explain the experiences and perspectives of rulers and subject peoples across the elaboration range for the chosen context: for Mongols — Kublai Khan as emperor of the Yuan Dynasty, use of diverse administrators, Marco Polo and trade; for Ottomans — the millet system, tolerance of Christians and Jews; for Vikings — attacks on monasteries, monks' written accounts, survival of Irish society under Viking and Norman contact, Dublin and Jorvik settlements; for Spanish conquest — encounters between Cortés and the Aztecs, siege of Tenochtitlan, impact of conquest on Indigenous populations and the wider world.
wider: For the Ottomans: analyse the millet system — regarding non-Muslim people as subjects but not subject to Muslim law — as a case study in how religious plurality was managed as a governance strategy, and compare this with the Spanish colonial approach

For the Vikings: examine the written accounts of monks that contributed to the Vikings' reputation for pillaging — questioning how this single-perspective source shapes historical understanding of Viking-subject encounters

For the Spanish conquest: investigate the encounters between Cortés and the Aztecs — examining how Aztec responses to Spanish power (including alliances with rival indigenous groups) shaped the outcome of the conquest

For the Vikings: investigate the remains of settlements at Dublin and Jorvik as archaeological evidence of cultural integration — showing how 'conquerors' and 'subject peoples' created hybrid societies
elaborations: describing the reign of Kublai Khan as the first Mongol emperor of China (the Yuan Dynasty), including the processes of government using administrators from different backgrounds and the growth of Chinese culture during this time
explaining the role of the Mongols in forging connections between Europe and Asia through conquest, settlement and trade, for example the meeting of Marco Polo and the development of trade
outlining the millet system that regarded non-Muslim people as subjects but as not being subject to Muslim law
explaining the tolerance of the Ottomans towards Christians and Jews
explaining the attacks on monasteries such as Lindisfarne (793 CE) and Iona (795 CE) and reviewing the written accounts of monks that contributed to the Vikings' reputation for pillaging and violence

explaining the survival of a heroic Iron Age society in early Medieval Ireland, as described in the vernacular epics, and its transformation by the spread of Christianity, the influence of the Vikings and the Anglo-Norman conquest
investigating the remains of Viking settlements such as Dublin (Ireland) and Jorvik (York)
The Spanish conquest of the Americas
describing encounters between Hernán Cortés and the Aztecs, as well as the siege of Tenochtitlan

investigating the impact of conquest on the Indigenous populations of the Americas (for example, the introduction of new diseases, horses and gunpowder, and the loss of natural resources) and the wider world (for example, the introduction of crops such as maize, beans, potatoes, tobacco and chocolate from the Americas to Europe and increased wealth in Europe)

AC9HH8K10.minimum_width: Explain the role and at least two achievements of one significant individual connected to empire or expansion — using at least one source as evidence.
AC9HH8K10.typical_width: Explain the role, achievements and significance of the chosen individual across the elaboration range: for Mongols — similarities and differences in leadership styles and successes of Genghis Khan and Kublai Khan; for Ottomans — historians' interpretations of Selim I or Suleiman the Magnificent; for Vikings — Erik the Red's settlements in Greenland; for Spanish conquest — key chronological events in the lives of Columbus, Balboa, Cortés, Montezuma II and/or Pizarro.
wider: Compare the leadership styles and successes of Genghis Khan (military expansion) and Kublai Khan (administrative consolidation) to show how different approaches to power can both be historically significant

Compare artefacts at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland with Viking artefacts as possible evidence that the Vikings journeyed to North America 500 years before Columbus — questioning who 'discovered' the Americas and what that framing reveals

Examine historians' interpretations of Selim I and Suleiman the Magnificent's achievements — comparing how the same individual's record can be assessed very differently depending on the interpretive lens used

Investigate how conquistadores such as Cortés or Pizarro have been interpreted differently — from heroic explorers to colonial oppressors — as a case study in how the same individual can be judged very differently depending on whose perspective is centred
elaborations: identifying the similarities in leadership styles and successes of Genghis Khan and Kublai Khan

comparing historians' interpretations of the achievements of individuals such as Selim I in establishing the empire and capturing Jerusalem, or Suleiman the Magnificent in expanding the empire to Belgrade in Europe
outlining Erik the Red's development of Viking settlements in Eastern and Western Greenland in 985 CE

comparing the artefacts discovered at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland (Canada) with Viking artefacts as possible evidence that the Vikings had journeyed to North America 500 years before Christopher Columbus
The Spanish conquest of the Americas
explaining the significance of key chronological events in the lives of individuals such as Columbus, Balboa, Cortés, Montezuma II and/or Pizarro

AC9HH8K11.minimum_width: Describe two different historical interpretations of the chosen empire or expansion — using at least one source type as evidence — and explain one reason why they differ.
AC9HH8K11.typical_width: Explain how and why historians have developed different interpretations across the elaboration range: validity of Mongol death toll estimates; contrasting perspectives on the Fall of Constantinople including prophecies and legends; the extent to which oral histories in Icelandic sagas are corroborated by evidence; the 'Gold, God and Glory' framework for Spanish conquest and how historians' interpretations of it differ.
wider: Examine contrasting perspectives on the Fall of Constantinople (1453) — including prophecies, legends and historical analysis — exploring how these shaped understanding of the experiences of people living through the event

Analyse the extent to which the 'Gold, God and Glory' framework holds for the Spanish conquest — examining how different historians weight religious, economic and political motivations and what evidence each draws on

Investigate the validity of Mongol death toll estimates (e.g. 1,000,000 in Nishapur, 60 million in China) using primary sources and historians' interpretations — exploring how demographic reasoning can be applied to evaluate extreme claims

Evaluate how post-colonial perspectives on the Spanish conquest have changed historical interpretations — particularly around the experiences of Indigenous peoples — examining what changed as Indigenous perspectives were included in the interpretive frame
elaborations: discussing the validity of various death tolls linked to Mongol expansion, such as 1,000,000 people in Nishapur and 60 million people in China, and using primary sources and historians' interpretations

describing the contrasting perspectives on the Fall of Constantinople (1453), including prophecies and legends, and how these shaped historians' interpretations of the experiences of people living at the time
analysing the extent to which historians' interpretations are corroborated with the oral histories contained in Icelandic sagas, such as about Erik the Red founding Greenland
The Spanish conquest of the Americas
analysing the extent to which historians' interpretations that the Spanish conquest can be attributed to the pursuit of "Gold, God and Glory" differ

AC9HH8K12.minimum_width: Describe at least two significant social, cultural, economic or political features of one Asia-Pacific society (Khmer Empire, feudal Japan or a Polynesian society) — explaining how these features shaped the way of life of different groups.
AC9HH8K12.typical_width: Explain the significant features of the chosen Asia-Pacific society across social, religious, cultural, economic and environmental dimensions. Cover the elaboration range for the chosen context: for Khmer — way of life as depicted through stone carvings and Zhou Daguan's writings (fishing, trading, temple construction); for feudal Japan — bushido, the social class hierarchy (emperor to workers) and cultural continuity; for Polynesia — the role of the ariki in Māori and Rapa Nui society, Rapa Nui clan structure, fishing, exchange of goods.
wider: For feudal Japan: examine how the relationship between different social classes — emperor, shogun, daimyo, samurai and workers — promoted social and cultural continuity across long periods of time, and why the hierarchy was stable
For Polynesian societies: compare the role of the ariki (chief) in Māori and Rapa Nui societies to examine how similar social structures produced different cultural practices across the Pacific

For Rapa Nui: investigate the way of life of Easter Island society — including fishing, clan exchange systems (goods, wives, labour), and use of stone tools — as an example of how small island societies organise complex social economies
For the Khmer: examine stone carvings and Zhou Daguan's account as two different source types for understanding Khmer daily life — comparing what each reveals and what each leaves invisible
elaborations: describing the way of life in the Khmer Empire as depicted through stone carvings and the writings of the Chinese Ambassador Zhou Daguan; for example, in relation to fishing, trading in markets, temple construction
Japan under the Shoguns

describing the way of life in feudal Japan under the shoguns; for example, "bushido" – the chivalric code of conduct of the samurai that emphasised frugality, loyalty, mastery of martial arts and honour
analysing how the relationship between the different social classes, such as the emperor, shogun, daimyo, samurai and workers, promoted social and cultural continuity
Polynesian expansion across the Pacific
describing the way of life in one Polynesian society, including the social, cultural, economic and political features, such as the role of the ariki in Māori and in Rapa Nui society

investigating the way of life of Easter Island (Rapa Nui) society; for example, fishing by the men; links between the household and the extended clan through the exchange of goods, wives and labour; the use of stone tools

AC9HH8K13.minimum_width: Explain one significant development or turning point in one Asia-Pacific society — describing at least two causes and at least two effects — and explain how it contributed to continuity and change.
AC9HH8K13.typical_width: Explain the chosen turning point across its full causal and consequential range for the selected context: for Khmer — theories of decline (climate instability, Theravada Buddhism, water management failure, Tai invasions), archaeological and paleo-environmental evidence of drought; for feudal Japan — Japan's closure to foreigners under the Tokugawa Shogunate, the role of the daimyo in ending the Ashikaga Shogunate, Perry's visit (1853); for Polynesia — theories of expansion (west-east vs east-west, accidental vs intentional), moai construction and transport, significance of Rahui, environmental challenges on different islands.
wider: For the Khmer: examine how archaeologists and paleo-environmentalists have established the prevalence of 14th–15th century droughts and their impact on the empire — using this as a case study in how environmental science contributes to historical understanding

For the moai: investigate the construction and transport of moai — techniques and theories about their meaning as representations of ancestors or chiefs — examining how monuments can reveal the values and capacities of a society

For Polynesia: examine the significance of Rahui as a way of prohibiting the collection of resources to ensure sustainability, exploring how this Indigenous environmental management practice responded to the decline and extinction of animals such as the moa

For feudal Japan: explain the reasons for Japan's closure to foreigners and the impact of Perry's visit (1853) — examining both the continuities maintained by isolation and the rapid change that isolation ultimately failed to prevent
elaborations: investigating theories about the decline of the Khmer Empire; for example, the development of an unstable climate such as drought and monsoons, the rise of Theravada Buddhism, the breakdown of Angkor's water management system

explaining how being revered as the "god-king" or "deva-raja" enabled the Khmer kings to rule over the empire with absolute authority, thereby enhancing their ability to mobilise the population to defend the empire as well as to invade neighbours
explaining the significance of the archaeological site of Angkor Wat as a demonstration of the empire's power
explaining how archaeologists and paleo-environmentalists have established the prevalence of droughts in the 14th–15th centuries and the impact of these droughts on the empire
Japan under the Shoguns
explaining reasons for Japan's closure to foreigners under the Tokugawa Shogunate and the impact of US Commodore Perry's visit in 1853
explaining the continuity of Shogunate power in areas such as trade, resource use and social classes

outlining the reasons for attempts by the Tokugawa Shogunate to curb deforestation, such as imposing heavy regulations on farmers, managing the harvesting of trees, and using new, lighter and more efficient construction techniques
explaining the role of the daimyo in contributing to the end of the Ashikaga Shogunate
Polynesian expansion across the Pacific
outlining different theories about the expansion; for example, west–east and east–west movements of settling peoples, and/or the expansion as accidental versus intentional

investigating the construction of the moai (giant statues) on Easter Island (Rapa Nui), the techniques used to make and transport them, and theories about their meaning, such as that they are representations of dead ancestors or chiefs
explaining the significance of Rahui as a way of prohibiting the collection of resources to ensure their sustainability as a response to the decline and extinction of animals such as the moa
explaining how environmental challenges were overcome on different islands to make settlement possible; for example, the practice of aquaculture in Nauru and/or agricultural practices in Hawaii

AC9HH8K14.minimum_width: Explain how rulers in one Asia-Pacific society exercised authority — using at least one source — and describe how at least one subject group experienced that authority.
AC9HH8K14.typical_width: Explain the experiences and perspectives of rulers and subject peoples across the elaboration range for the chosen context: for Khmer — perspectives of Angkor through stone carvings and Zhou Daguan's writings; for feudal Japan — the Tokugawa Shogunate reimposing a feudal system based on daimyo and samurai, impact on different classes; for Polynesia — artefacts (Lapita pottery, tapa cloth, ship-building) as insight into society, responsibilities and privileges of chiefs in New Zealand, Hawaii, Tonga and/or the Society Islands.
wider: For feudal Japan: examine the impact of the Tokugawa Shogunate's reimposition of the feudal system on merchants and artisans — whose wealth grew but whose formal status remained low — as a case study in how formal hierarchy and economic reality can diverge

For Polynesia: compare the responsibilities and privileges of chiefs across different societies (Māori, Hawaiian, Tongan) to examine how chiefly authority varied in its form and functions across the Pacific

For the Khmer: examine how the god-king's authority was both sustained and challenged by his obligation to deliver prosperity — when environmental failure disrupted the water management system, the basis of royal authority was threatened

For Polynesia: examine artefacts (Lapita pottery from Vanuatu, tapa cloth, ship-building techniques) as evidence of the daily life and capabilities of ordinary Polynesian peoples — not just their rulers
elaborations: analysing the perspectives of Angkor as depicted through stone carvings and the writings of Chinese Ambassador Zhou Daguan; for example, in relation to fishing, trading in markets and temple construction
Japan under the Shoguns
discussing the role of the Tokugawa Shogunate in reimposing a feudal system (based on daimyo and samurai) and explaining the impact of this change on the daily life of different classes
Polynesian expansion across the Pacific
examining artefacts such as Lapita pottery from Vanuatu, tapa cloth and/or ship-building techniques to provide insight into those societies
describing the responsibilities and privileges of being a chief in a society such as those in New Zealand, Hawaii, Tonga and/or the Society Islands

AC9HH8K15.minimum_width: Explain the role and at least two achievements of one significant individual or group in one Asia-Pacific society — using at least one source as evidence.
AC9HH8K15.typical_width: Explain the role, achievements and significance of the chosen individual or group across the elaboration range: for Khmer — Jayavarman VII's rule, expansion of the empire, expulsion of the Chams, scale of the Angkor construction program; for feudal Japan — the legacy of Tokugawa Ieyasu as founder of the Edo Shogunate; for Polynesia — the achievements of one Polynesian group (Māori, Samoan, Tahitian, Tongan or Rapa Nui) in navigation, settlement and cultural development.
wider: For the Khmer: examine Jayavarman VII's building program as both a demonstration of imperial power and a potential source of the empire's later fragility — asking whether great achievement can contain the seeds of decline

For Polynesia: describe the achievements of one Polynesian group and evaluate what these reveal about the capabilities and values of Pacific peoples — connecting their historical achievements to contemporary cultural identity

For feudal Japan: examine the legacy of Tokugawa Ieyasu in shaping Japan's political culture — tracing how the Edo Shogunate's structures both enabled Japan's stability and created the conditions that made the Meiji Restoration necessary

Compare the achievements of Jayavarman VII (military expansion and construction) with Tokugawa Ieyasu (political consolidation) to explore how different forms of achievement — conquest vs governance — leave different kinds of legacy
elaborations: describing the rule of Jayavarman VII and his influence in expanding the empire, expelling the Chams and on the scale of the construction program in Angkor
Japan under the Shoguns
explaining the legacy of Tokugawa Ieyasu as founder of the Edo Shogunate
Polynesian expansion across the Pacific
describing the achievements of one Polynesian group of people such as Māori, Samoan, Tahitian (Maohi), Tongans or Rapa Nui

AC9HH8K16.minimum_width: Describe two different interpretations of the chosen Asia-Pacific society — and explain one reason why they differ, with reference to source challenges or evidential limitations.
AC9HH8K16.typical_width: Explain how and why historians have developed different interpretations across the elaboration range: theories about the causes of the Khmer Empire's decline (Tai invasions, building program, population growth, religious revolution, environmental challenges, water management failure); the significance of Japan's closure to foreigners and Perry's visit; the challenges posed by the lack of written sources for Polynesian history — including changes in interpretations of Lapita culture in Vanuatu.
wider: Discuss the multiple theories for the Khmer decline — examining how each is supported by different types of evidence (political, religious, environmental, archaeological) and why no single explanation is universally accepted

Evaluate the significance of competing theories about Polynesian expansion — considering what is at stake in the debate between accidental and intentional navigation for how Pacific peoples' agency and capability are understood

Examine the challenges posed by the lack of written sources for Polynesian history — using changes in interpretations of Lapita culture as a concrete example of how new evidence can overturn established interpretations

Evaluate the range of reasons for Japan's closure to foreigners under the Tokugawa Shogunate — and assess the impact of Perry's visit (1853) by comparing interpretations that frame isolation as a strength vs interpretations that frame it as a vulnerability
elaborations: discussing theories about the causes of and/or the factors that contributed to the decline of the Khmer Empire; for example, Tai invasions, economic decline as a result of Jayavarman VII's building program, population growth and attempts to control trade routes, religious revolution through the rise of Theravada Buddhism, internal political tension, environmental challenges such as soil sterilisation, over-intensified land use, the development of an unstable climate through drought and monsoons, and the breakdown of Angkor's water management system
Japan under the Shoguns
evaluating the significance of the range of reasons for Japan's closure to foreigners under the Tokugawa Shogunate and the impact of US Commodore Perry's visit in 1853
Polynesian expansion across the Pacific
explaining the challenges posed by the lack of written sources in understanding the history of Polynesia, such as changes in interpretations of Lapita culture being present in Vanuatu

AC9HH8S01.minimum_width: Develop one key historical question framed to invite explanation (why/how) about a specific historical context, and at least two supporting sub-questions about evidence or theories.
AC9HH8S01.typical_width: Develop a multi-level question hierarchy: a key inquiry question; related sub-questions about evidence ('What evidence is there?', 'What theories have been developed?'); questions about historical significance with measurable criteria (scale, duration, depth of change); review and revise questions when unexpected or challenging developments arise during the investigation.
wider: Develop multiple candidate key questions for the same inquiry and evaluate which is best scoped — identifying what each question foregrounds, what it leaves out, and which would best direct a productive investigation

Practice reviewing questions at multiple points in an inquiry — identifying what the initial question assumed, what investigation revealed, and how the question should be revised to reflect more accurate historical understanding

Apply question development to a topic where the evidence is partial or contested (e.g. Polynesian expansion theories, Khmer decline) — developing questions that acknowledge evidential uncertainty rather than assuming a settled historical record
elaborations: developing a key question such as "How did the decline of Rome's western empire change the organisation of European society?" or "Why did Easter Island (Rapa Nui) society decline?"; identifying related questions to inform the inquiry, such as "What evidence is there?" and "What theories have been developed?"
developing questions about historical significance such as "How many people were affected by the Black Death?" and "How long did it last?"

reviewing questions when faced with unexpected or challenging developments posed by the historical investigation; for example, "How was the organisation of Japanese society influenced by world events?"

AC9HH8S02.minimum_width: Locate at least two sources of different types (e.g. one written, one visual or artefact), correctly categorise them as primary or secondary, and retrieve relevant information from at least one digital source.
AC9HH8S02.typical_width: Organise sources into systematic categories (primary/secondary; written, visual, material culture, artefacts) with examples from each category relevant to the inquiry; retrieve relevant information from multiple digital sources — including repositories, maps and photographs of artefacts — using advanced search functions to refine results.
wider: Compare two searches on the same topic using different strategies (broad vs specific terms, with vs without filters) to examine how search design affects the quality of retrieved sources

Investigate how to locate primary sources from non-European medieval societies (e.g. Islamic manuscripts, Chinese diplomatic records, Icelandic sagas) using digital repositories — examining how the availability of digitised sources varies by culture and period

Apply the source categorisation framework to a source that is genuinely ambiguous (e.g. Boccaccio's Decameron — literary but also primary evidence of attitudes) to practise reasoning about edge cases in the primary/secondary distinction
elaborations: organising sources into categories such as primary and secondary sources and/or written, visual, material culture, and artefacts; for example, sources from the period investigated including journals, church records, paintings, artefacts, and sites and sources written after the period including fictional and artistic interpretations, and academic texts

retrieving relevant information from multiple digital sources, including repositories of primary sources, maps and photographs of culturally significant artefacts such as online platforms, and using advanced search functions to refine the search

AC9HH8S03.minimum_width: Apply the four source analysis questions (who, when, why, what does it show) to at least two sources of different types, with substantive answers — not just labelling.
AC9HH8S03.typical_width: Systematically apply four-question analysis to a range of source types (photographs, artefacts, stories, buildings); use internal clues (place found, materials, condition, decorative features) to infer where a source was made or who made it; discuss at least one source where origin or purpose is difficult to determine and explain how this uncertainty affects its usefulness.
wider: Apply provenance inference to Polynesian artefacts such as Lapita pottery — using clay composition, decoration and find site to make inferences about the movements and contacts of Polynesian peoples
Examine Viking craft (weapons, armour, longboats) and use design features to infer when and where items were made and what they reveal about the society's values and capabilities

Investigate the Icelandic sagas as a source type with genuinely uncertain origin — examining where archaeological and saga accounts align and diverge, and what this means for how the sagas can be used as historical evidence

Apply the four questions to illuminated manuscripts as sources — examining how the monastic scribes' preservation of ancient texts constitutes evidence of medieval scholarly values as well as a record of classical knowledge
elaborations: responding to questions such as "Who wrote/produced this?", "When?", "Why?" and "What does it show about the past?" about photographs, artefacts, stories, buildings and other sources to explain the past

explaining how clues within a source can be used to identify where it was made or who it was made by; for example, the place where it was found, the materials used, the condition of the object, decorative features
discussing the difficulty of identifying the origin and purpose of some sources, and how this can impact on the source's usefulness

AC9HH8S04.minimum_width: Examine the validity of at least one source using the four validity questions (where does it come from, what information is provided, is it fact or opinion, what other sources are needed) and correctly distinguish at least two factual statements from two opinion statements.
AC9HH8S04.typical_width: Systematically examine source validity using the four validity questions; distinguish fact from opinion using linguistic strategies — identifying conditionals ('might', 'could'), hedging words ('believe', 'think', 'suggests') and evaluative language; evaluate the usefulness of at least one source for a specific inquiry question — explaining how accuracy, origin and purpose affect what the source can contribute.
wider: Evaluate the usefulness of multiple sources covering the same event (e.g. Matteo Villani's diary, Boccaccio's Decameron, Ibn Khaldun's recollections) for the same inquiry question — examining how different sources are useful in different ways for the same question

Apply the fact-opinion distinction to a source with contested provenance (e.g. a chronicle of uncertain authorship) — examining how provenance uncertainty compounds the difficulty of assessing factual content

Examine how historians deliberately use hedging language to signal evidential uncertainty — distinguishing this from weak argument — and practise incorporating appropriate hedging in students' own historical writing

Evaluate the usefulness of church records as evidence of Black Death mortality — examining who kept the records, why, and what they may have omitted or exaggerated, as a case study in how validity assessment depends on understanding institutional context
elaborations: examining the validity of sources by asking questions such as "Where does it come from?", "What information is provided?", "Is the information factual or an opinion?" and "What other sources may be needed to support/challenge this source?"

distinguishing between fact (for example, "The moai were constructed on Easter Island [Rapa Nui]") and opinion or interpretation (for example, "The moai on Easter Island [Rapa Nui] are representations of gods")

using strategies to detect whether a statement is fact or opinion, including word choices that may indicate an opinion is being offered; for example, the use of conditionals "might" and "could", and words such as "believe", "think" and "suggests"

AC9HH8S05.minimum_width: Sequence at least three historical events to identify a broader pattern of cause/effect or change/continuity, and describe at least one continuity with reference to what specifically persisted — not just 'nothing changed'.
AC9HH8S05.typical_width: Sequence historical events to identify broader patterns across multiple domains; explain observations with reference to key events, individuals, themes and sources; describe continuities with precision — highlighting lack of deviation, widespread similarity, and structural persistence; distinguish structural continuity from the diminishing significance of a short-term development.
wider: Apply precise continuity description to the Tokugawa Shogunate's isolation policy — identifying what remained structurally continuous across the period of isolation, what changed at the surface level, and how Perry's arrival challenged both

Examine continuity in Polynesian cultural practices (navigation, social organisation, exchange systems) across different island societies — showing how cultural continuity can span geographic dispersal
Apply the four dimensions of change (quality, type, speed, impact) to the Black Death — examining how different dimensions foreground different aspects of what changed and what continued

Compare the pace and scope of change in two different medieval contexts (e.g. feudal Europe vs Tokugawa Japan) using the same continuity-and-change framework — developing transferable analytical language for comparing historical rates of change
elaborations: sequencing historical events to identify broader patterns of cause and/or effect, and change and/or continuity across society, and explaining their observations with reference to key events, individuals, themes and sources of evidence

describing continuities by highlighting the lack of deviation, the similarities of important aspects, and the widespread nature of similarities in the era, period or society despite an event, idea, person, group or movement achieving short-term significance

AC9HH8S06.minimum_width: Identify at least two values or attitudes revealed by one source and explain what these suggest about the source's producer. Use at least one additional source to assess how representative those values are.
AC9HH8S06.typical_width: Identify values and attitudes revealed by individual sources across multiple source types; use additional sources to show whether an account's values are broadly representative of or contrast with wider societal values; explain why historians have different interpretations — including access to source material, personal views and contextual factors of the historian's own time.
wider: Compare the values revealed by sources from different social groups about the same event (e.g. aristocratic vs peasant accounts of feudal society, or monastic vs secular accounts of the Vikings) — showing how societal values are contested across class and position

Examine how post-colonial historians' interpretations of the Spanish conquest have changed as Indigenous perspectives were included — identifying what changed about whose values were centred in the historical account
Investigate how feminist historiography has changed interpretations of Renaissance women — examining what values the earlier historiography reflected and what values drove the revision

Apply values and attitudes analysis to a non-European source (e.g. Zhou Daguan's account of the Khmer, Ibn Khaldun's plague recollection) — examining how the values of an outside observer shape what they notice, record and omit
elaborations: describing the values and attitudes revealed by a source such as an individual account, and using additional sources to show how they are broadly representative or contrast the values and attitudes of the society

identifying the perspective in a source and discussing the values and attitudes of the society that produced it; for example, explaining why historians have different interpretations, including access to source material, personal views and other contextual factors influencing the time in which the historian was working

AC9HH8S07.minimum_width: Identify two different historical interpretations of one significant event, individual or group — accurately describing what each claims — and explain at least one specific reason why they differ.
AC9HH8S07.typical_width: Identify and explain differing historians' interpretations across the elaboration range: short-term triggers vs longer-term causes of a significant event; different interpretations of the influence of scientific ideas or the status of women; use interpretations to describe change in terms of quality, type, speed and impact.
wider: Identify interpretations of the same event from historians working in different periods or traditions (e.g. 19th-century European accounts of the Spanish conquest vs 21st-century post-colonial accounts) — showing how interpretations are historically situated

Apply the four dimensions of change (quality, type, speed, impact) to competing interpretations of the Black Death — examining how different interpretations foreground different dimensions of what changed
Map the full range of interpretations of a complex event (e.g. the decline of the Khmer Empire) — showing that the interpretive field is not just binary but contains multiple overlapping frameworks

Examine the distinction between short-term triggers and longer-term structural causes using a specific event (e.g. the fall of Constantinople, or Viking decline) — developing this as a transferable analytical tool for interpreting historical debates
elaborations: identifying differing historians' interpretations on the short-term triggers and longer-term causes of a significant event
identifying different interpretations of an event or development, such as the influence of scientific ideas or the status of women, and accounting for the differences
using historical interpretations to describe change in relation to quality, type, speed and impact

AC9HH8S08.minimum_width: Write a piece of historical writing with an argument-focused introduction, body paragraphs that reference source evidence, and a conclusion that restates the argument — using at least four historical terms or concepts accurately.
AC9HH8S08.typical_width: Create historical descriptions, explanations and arguments across the full elaboration range: use structural elements for argumentative effect (introduction outlining the argument, conclusion summarising and restating it); present historical findings in at least one format appropriate to audience and purpose (podcast, oral presentation, essay); apply historical terms and concepts in their appropriate historical context.
wider: Develop the same historical argument for two different formats (e.g. an essay and a podcast script) — identifying what changes and what stays the same, and examining how format shapes but does not determine the argument

Practise writing argument-focused introductions by comparing a topic-introduction and an argument-introduction for the same question — explaining why the second is more effective for historical writing

Apply historical terminology from across the Y8 curriculum (e.g. turning point, continuity, feudalism, deva-raja, bushido, Encomienda, millet system) in extended writing — practising the distinction between using terms as labels vs using them to do analytical work

Examine how historical documentaries or museum exhibits communicate historical knowledge and argument — evaluating their effectiveness against the criteria applied to written historical argument and identifying what different formats can and cannot do
elaborations: communicating explanations or analysis using structural elements for effect; for example, an introduction that outlines an argument and a conclusion that summarises and restates the argument
presenting findings or historical knowledge in range of formats, such as a podcast, an oral presentation or an essay, appropriate to audience and purpose with reference to evidence
developing descriptions and explanations, applying historical terms and concepts in their appropriate historical context
